mainTopic: The end of the יפת תואר דרשות, then the conditions for piercing an עבד עברי and the master's duties to him and his family
overview: This amud finishes the Torah's rules about the יפת תואר, the captive woman taken in war. The Torah permits her only as a lesser evil, and each word of the פסוק adds a limit: one woman only, only for himself, marriage can take effect, and nothing until he brings her home. Then a ברייתא teaches that an עבד עברי who wants to stay must say 'I love my master' twice. רבא explains that both statements are tied to his last פרוטה of work. A second ברייתא requires that servant and master match: both have a wife and children, they love each other, and neither one alone is sick. רב ביבי בר אביי asks about the case where both are sick, and the question ends in תיקו. The גמרא then learns from 'כי טוב לו עמך' that the servant must eat, drink and sleep as well as his master, so buying a עבד עברי is like buying a master. Finally, רבי שמעון teaches that the master must also feed the servant's wife and children, and the גמרא shows why both cases are needed. The amud ends as a new ברייתא begins.

steps.title: Better slaughtered dying animals than carcasses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its explanation of why the Torah allows the יפת תואר: a controlled permission is better than a full sin.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is better that they eat meat of dying animals that were properly slaughtered, and not eat meat of dying animals that die by themselves and become carcasses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a comparison it started on the previous page. It explains why the Torah permits the יפת תואר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah is speaking against the יצר הרע of a soldier in war. If he will act on his desire anyway, it is better he does it in a permitted way, like slaughtering a dying animal, than in a fully forbidden way, like eating a נבלה.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals that are about to die
Animals that died without שחיטה, forbidden to eat
The captive woman a soldier may take in war

steps.confusionAlert: The Torah is not praising this act. It is a reluctant permission so the soldier does not end up doing something worse.

phrases.english: dying animals that were slaughtered,
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous page: 'It is better that Jews eat meat of...'

phrases.english: and let them not eat the meat of
dying animals that become carcasses.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּמוּתוֹת שְׁחוּטוֹת, וְאַל יֹאכְלוּ בְּשַׂר תְּמוּתוֹת נְבֵילוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a parable begun before this section about why the Torah permits יפת תואר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Torah permits יפת תואר as a lesser evil, like slaughtering a dying animal rather than eating it as a נבלה.

steps.title: Even if she is not pretty, and only one woman
steps.stepSummary: Two lessons from the words 'וחשקת' and 'בה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And you desire' teaches that this applies even if she is not pretty. 'Her' teaches: her, and not her together with another woman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts reading the פסוק of יפת תואר word by word. Each word gives a new detail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'וחשקת' makes the rule depend on the soldier's own desire, not on how beautiful she really is. 'בה' (her) is singular, so he may take only one captive this way.

phrases.english: "And you desire"
even if she is not pretty.
"Her"
and not her and her friend.
phrases.notes: He may take only one captive woman this way, not two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After explaining why the permission exists, the גמרא now sets out its limits from the words of the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rule applies even if she is not pretty, and he may take only one woman.

steps.title: Marriage takes effect, but not one for a father or son
steps.stepSummary: Lessons from 'ולקחת' and 'לך לאשה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And you shall take' teaches that marriage can take effect with her. 'For you as a wife' teaches that he may not take two women, one for himself and one for his father, or one for himself and one for his son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps reading the פסוק. It learns two more details about the יפת תואר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ולקחת' is the Torah's word for marriage, so a real marriage can take effect with her. 'לך' (for you) means only for himself, so he cannot take a second captive for a father or son.

phrases.english: "And you shall take"
you have taking with her.
phrases.notes: 'Taking' is the Torah's word for marriage, so a real marriage can take effect with her.

phrases.english: "For you as a wife"
that he may not take two women,
one for him and one for his father,
one for him and one for his son.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the word-by-word reading of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קידושין takes effect with a יפת תואר, and he may not take a second one for a father or son.

steps.title: Not on the battlefield
steps.stepSummary: From 'והבאתה' we learn he must first bring her home.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And you shall bring her' teaches that he may not press her during the war.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last word the גמרא reads in the יפת תואר section. It sets a rule about timing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says he brings her into his house first. So he may not force himself on her right there in the war; the whole process happens at home.
steps.whatToRemember: Each word of the יפת תואר פסוק adds a limit: one woman, only for himself, marriage can take effect, and nothing until he brings her home.

phrases.english: "And you shall bring her"
teaches that he should not press her during the war.
phrases.notes: He means he may not force himself on her on the battlefield. First he brings her home.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final derivation in the יפת תואר list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He may not be with her during the war. He must first bring her home.

steps.title: The slave must say it twice
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: the double word 'אמר יאמר' teaches that the עבד עברי must make his statement twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'If he shall surely say.' He is not pierced until he says it and says it again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: the עבד עברי who wants to stay with his master. This line sets up the two cases that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah could have written 'יאמר' once, but it wrote 'אמר יאמר'. The ברייתא reads the double word as two separate statements, both needed before רציעה.

keyTerms.meaning: If he shall surely say (a doubled verb)
A Jewish slave who works for six years

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"If he shall surely say"
phrases.notes: שמות 21:5. In Hebrew the word 'say' appears twice.

phrases.english: until he says and repeats.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״אִם אָמֹר יֹאמַר״ – עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר וְיִשְׁנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. The יפת תואר discussion ends and the ברייתא on the נרצע begins.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עבד עברי is pierced only if he says 'I love my master' twice.

steps.title: Saying it only early is not enough
steps.stepSummary: If he said it during his years of work but not at the end, he is not pierced.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said it at the beginning of the six years but not at the end of the six, he is not pierced, because it says 'I will not go out free', meaning he must say it at the time he goes out.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the first of the two required times. It shows that a statement made only early on does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'I will not go out free' only make sense when he is actually about to go out. So a statement made only earlier is missing the second required moment.

keyTerms.meaning: At the beginning of the six years
At the end of the six years
Pierced through the ear, so he stays a slave longer
At the time of going out free

phrases.english: If he said at the beginning of six
phrases.notes: At first this sounds like early in his six years. In step 10, רבא explains it means the start of his very last פרוטה of work.

phrases.english: and did not say at the end of six,
he is not pierced,
as it is said: "I will not go out free"
until he says it at the time of going out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר בִּתְחִילַּת שֵׁשׁ וְלֹא אָמַר בְּסוֹף שֵׁשׁ – אֵינוֹ נִרְצָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains what 'saying twice' requires: one of the two times must be at the end.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying it only during the years, without saying it at the end, does not make him נרצע.

steps.title: Saying it only at the end is not enough
steps.stepSummary: If he said it only at the end of the six years, he is not pierced, because he must say it while still a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said it at the end of the six but not at the beginning of the six, he is not pierced, because it says 'If the slave shall surely say', meaning he must say it while he is still a slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the opposite case. A statement made only at the very end also does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls him 'the slave' when he speaks. At the very end of six years his time is up, so the ברייתא requires a statement while he is clearly still a slave, too. Together the two cases explain the two statements of 'אמר יאמר'.

keyTerms.meaning: While he is still a slave
The piercing of the slave's ear

steps.whatToRemember: An עבד עברי becomes נרצע only if he says 'I love my master' twice: once while he is still a slave and once at the end, when he would go out. רבא explains in step 10 that both mean his very last פרוטה of work: its start and its end.

phrases.english: If he said at the end of six
and did not say at the beginning of six,
he is not pierced,
as it is said: "If the slave shall surely say"
until he says it while he is a slave.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר בְּסוֹף שֵׁשׁ וְלֹא אָמַר בִּתְחִילַּת שֵׁשׁ – אֵינוֹ נִרְצָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror case of step 6. Together they define both required statements.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Saying it only at the end, without saying it during his years as a slave, does not make him נרצע.

steps.title: Why not learn this from "I love my wife and children"?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's rule that a statement made only at the beginning of the six years does not count. It asks why the ברייתא needs the פסוק "I will not go out free" when another requirement already rules this case out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: If he said it at the beginning of the six years but not at the end, he is not pierced, because it says "I will not go out free." Why learn it from that? Learn it from the fact that he must be able to say "I love my master, my wife, and my children," and at the beginning he can't say that!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the ברייתא in Step 6 and questions its proof. It suggests a simpler source for the same rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At the start of his six years, the servant does not yet have children from the שפחה כנענית his master gave him. So he cannot truthfully say "I love my children." That alone should disqualify him, so why does the ברייתא need the words "I will not go out free"?

keyTerms.meaning: Why specifically this? Why pick this source over another?
Let him derive it (from a different, simpler source)
Pierced: the servant's ear is pierced and he stays on as a servant

phrases.english: The Master said:
If he said it at the beginning of the six years
and did not say it at the end of the six years,
he is not pierced,
as it says: "I will not go out free."
Why learn it specifically from "I will not go out free"?
Let him learn it from the fact that we require:

phrases.aramaic: ״אָהַבְתִּי אֶת אֲדֹנִי אֶת אִשְׁתִּי וְאֶת בָּנָי״
phrases.english: "I love my master, my wife, and my children"
and that is missing!
phrases.notes: At the start of his six years he doesn't have children yet from the שפחה his master gave him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִירְיָא, מִ״לֹּא אֵצֵא חׇפְשִׁי״? תִּיפּוֹק לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא's rule from Step 6 and questions its source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of "I will not go out free" for the case of saying it only at the beginning
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A simpler disqualifier exists: at the beginning he has no children, so he cannot say "I love my children."

steps.title: Isn't he still a slave at the end of six years?
steps.stepSummary: A second question on the ברייתא: it says a statement made only at the end doesn't count because the פסוק says "the slave." But at the end of six years he is still a slave!
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore: if he said it at the end of six but not at the beginning, he is not pierced, because it says "the slave." Is he not a slave at the end of six?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a second difficulty with the ברייתא, this time on the rule from Step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said the word "the slave" means he must speak while still a slave. But the end of the six years is still part of his time as a slave. So this proof seems not to work.

keyTerms.meaning: And furthermore: introduces a second question
Is that to say? Introduces a question that points out something seemingly wrong
"The slave": the word in the פסוק that the ברייתא uses as its proof

phrases.english: And furthermore,
if he said it at the end of the six years
and did not say it at the beginning of the six years,
he is not pierced,
as it says "the slave."

phrases.aramaic: אַטּוּ סוֹף שֵׁשׁ לָאו עֶבֶד הוּא?
phrases.english: Is he not a slave at the end of the six years?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second question on the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's proof from "the slave" for the case of saying it only at the end
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: At the end of six years he is still a slave, so the word "the slave" should not exclude him.

steps.title: רבא: both times refer to the last פרוטה of work
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that "beginning of six" means the start of the last פרוטה's worth of work, and "end of six" means after that last פרוטה is finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: "At the beginning of six" means at the beginning of the last פרוטה. "At the end of six" means at the end of the last פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers both questions by explaining what the ברייתא really means by "beginning" and "end."
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Beginning" is not the first day; it is the start of his very last bit of work, when he already has his family and is still a slave. That answers Step 8, since he can say "I love my children" then. "End" means after the last פרוטה is done, when he is already free. That answers Step 9, since then he truly is no longer "the slave."

keyTerms.meaning: The last פרוטה: the final small amount of work still owed before he goes free

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read "beginning of six" as the first year. Here it means the start of the very last moment of service, right before he goes free.
steps.whatToRemember: The servant must say his statement twice: once just before his time ends (while still a slave), and once at the very end. Saying it only after he is already free does not count.

phrases.english: רבא said:
What does "at the beginning of six" mean?
At the beginning of the last פרוטה.
phrases.notes: He means the start of the very last bit of work, worth one פרוטה, that he still owes.

phrases.english: And what does "at the end of six" mean?
At the end of the last פרוטה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers both questions from Steps 8 and 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the terms in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: "Beginning" and "end" meant the start and end of the full six-year period.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both terms refer to the last פרוטה: "beginning" is still slavery with a family; "end" is already freedom.

steps.title: Both servant and master must have a wife and children
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא: if only one of them, the servant or the master, has a wife and children, the servant is not pierced.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If the servant has a wife and children but his master does not, he is not pierced, because it says "for he loves you and your house." If the master has a wife and children but the servant does not, he is not pierced, because it says "I love my master, my wife, and my children."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא listing conditions for רציעה. This first part is about family.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Your house" means the master's wife and children, so the master needs a family. "My wife and my children" means the servant needs a family too. Both פסוקים must be true.

keyTerms.meaning: Your house: here it means the master's family

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If he has a wife and children
and his master does not have a wife and children,
he is not pierced,
as it says: "For he loves you and your house."
If his master has a wife and children
and he does not have a wife and children,
he is not pierced,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אָהַבְתִּי אֶת אֲדֹנִי אֶת אִשְׁתִּי וְאֶת בָּנָי״.
phrases.english: as it says: "I love my master, my wife, and my children."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ברייתא about other conditions for רציעה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both the servant and the master must have a wife and children for רציעה.

steps.title: The love must go both ways
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: if only one of them loves the other, the servant is not pierced.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he loves his master but his master does not love him, he is not pierced, because it says "for it is good for him with you." If his master loves him but he does not love his master, he is not pierced, because it says "for he loves you."
steps.whatsHappening: The same ברייתא adds a second condition: the love must be mutual.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Good for him with you" shows the relationship must be good for both sides, so the master must love him too. "He loves you" shows the servant must love the master.

keyTerms.meaning: "For it is good for him with you" (דברים 15:16)

phrases.english: If he loves his master
but his master does not love him,
he is not pierced,
as it says: "For it is good for him with you."
If his master loves him
but he does not love his master,
he is not pierced,
as it says: "For he loves you."

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא אוֹהֵב אֶת רַבּוֹ וְרַבּוֹ אֵינוֹ אוֹהֲבוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with the condition of mutual love.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Servant and master must love each other for רציעה.

steps.title: Both must be in the same state of health
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends: if only one of them is sick, the servant is not pierced.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is sick and his master is not, he is not pierced, because it says "for it is good for him with you." If his master is sick and he is not, he is not pierced, because it says "with you."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its list with a condition about health.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sick servant is not someone for whom "it is good," so he can't be pierced. "With you" teaches that the two must be alike, so if only the master is sick, the servant is also not pierced.

keyTerms.meaning: "With you": teaches that servant and master must be in a similar situation

steps.whatToRemember: For רציעה, servant and master must match: both have families, both love each other, and both are healthy. If only one of them is sick, there is no רציעה. The case where both are sick comes up in the next step and stays unresolved (תיקו).

phrases.english: If he is sick and his master is not sick,
he is not pierced,
as it says: "For it is good for him with you."
If his master is sick and he is not sick,
he is not pierced,
as it says: "With you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא's list with the condition of health.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If only one of them is sick, there is no רציעה.

steps.title: What if both the servant and the master are sick?
steps.stepSummary: רב ביבי בר אביי asks whether the servant can be pierced when both he and his master are sick.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ביבי בר אביי asked: if both of them are sick, what is the law? Is the requirement only that the servant be 'with you,' meaning in the same condition as the master? That is true here. Or is the requirement 'it is good for him with you'? That is not true here.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא said that if only one of them is sick, there is no piercing. Now רב ביבי בר אביי asks about a case where both are sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question depends on how to read the פסוק. If the key word is just 'עמך' (being equal with the master), then two sick people are equal and the servant can be pierced. If the key is 'כי טוב לו עמך' (things are good for him), then two sick people do not have a good situation, so there is no piercing.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (raised a question that needs an answer)
With you, meaning equal to the master
For it is good for him with you (דברים 15:16)

phrases.english: Rav Beivai bar Abaye asked:
If both of them are sick, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'Both of them' means the servant and the master, like in the last part of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: Do we require only "with you"
and that is present here,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִילְמָא ״כִּי טוֹב לוֹ עִמָּךְ״ בָּעֵינַן –
phrases.english: or perhaps we require "for it is good for him with you"
and that is missing here?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the ruling that if only one of them is sick there is no piercing, and asks about the case where both are sick.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the פסוק require only that servant and master be in the same condition, or that the situation actually be good for the servant?

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: No answer is found, so the question of two sick people is left open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand. (The question stays unanswered.)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא cannot settle רב ביבי בר אביי's question, so it leaves it open.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No source decides between the two readings of the פסוק. 'תיקו' means the question stands without an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand. The question stays unresolved.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question asked in step 14 without an answer.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whether a servant can be pierced when both he and his master are sick stays an open question.

steps.title: The servant must live as well as the master
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from 'כי טוב לו עמך' that the master must give the servant food, drink, and bedding equal to his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'For it is good for him with you' means he must be with you in food and with you in drink. You may not eat fine bread while he eats coarse bread. You may not drink aged wine while he drinks new wine. You may not sleep on soft bedding while he sleeps on straw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that uses the same phrase 'כי טוב לו עמך' to teach how a master must treat his עבד עברי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the phrase was a condition for piercing. Here the same words teach an everyday duty: the servant's standard of living must match the master's. The three examples (bread, wine, bedding) show this covers food, drink, and sleep.

keyTerms.meaning: Fine bread made from clean flour

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"For it is good for him with you"
with you in food,
with you in drink.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא תְּהֵא אַתָּה אוֹכֵל פַּת נְקִיָּה
phrases.english: So that you should not be eating fine bread
while he eats coarse bran bread,
you drinking aged wine
while he drinks new wine,
you sleeping on soft bedding
while he sleeps on straw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the same phrase from the previous question but uses it for a new law about how the servant is treated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A master must give his עבד עברי food, drink, and bedding of the same quality as his own.

steps.title: Buying a servant is like buying a master
steps.stepSummary: From this duty of equal treatment, the חכמים say that whoever buys a עבד עברי is like someone buying a master for himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: From here they said: anyone who buys a Hebrew servant is like one who buys a master for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with a famous saying that sums up the rule it just taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the master must give the servant food, drink, and bedding equal to his own, he can never live better than his servant. The owner has to keep looking after the servant's comfort, which is why it feels like buying a master.
steps.whatToRemember: Because of 'כי טוב לו עמך,' a עבד עברי must live as well as his master. That is why 'כל הקונה עבד עברי כקונה אדון לעצמו.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This well-known line shows that the Torah's servant laws are built to protect the servant's dignity.

phrases.english: From here they said:
Anyone who buys a Hebrew servant
is like one who buys a master for himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general saying from the equal-treatment rule in step 16.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Owning a עבד עברי puts heavy duties on the owner, so it is like taking a master for oneself.

steps.title: The master must feed the servant's children
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון learns from 'he and his children with him' that the master has to support the servant's children.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: 'And he shall go out from you, he and his children with him.' רבי שמעון said: if he was sold, were his sons and daughters sold? From here we learn that his master must feed his children.
steps.whatsHappening: A new ברייתא: רבי שמעון notices a strange phrase in the פסוק and learns a new law from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The children were never sold, so why would the Torah say they 'go out' with him? רבי שמעון explains that while the father serves, the master is responsible for feeding the children. When the father goes free, that support ends, and that is what the פסוק means by 'going out.'

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
"And he shall go out from you,
he and his children with him,"
Rabbi Shimon said:
If he was sold,
were his sons and daughters sold?
From here we learn that his master is obligated
to feed his children.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״וְיָצָא מֵעִמָּךְ הוּא וּבָנָיו עִמּוֹ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of the master's duties to his servant and adds his duty to the servant's family.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The master of a עבד עברי must support the servant's children.

steps.title: The master must also feed the servant's wife
steps.stepSummary: Using the same reasoning on 'his wife shall go out with him,' רבי שמעון learns that the master must support the servant's wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the same way you say: 'If he is married, his wife shall go out with him.' רבי שמעון said: if he was sold, was his wife sold? From here we learn that his master must feed his wife.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא repeats the same kind of reasoning on a second פסוק, this time about the servant's wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wife was never sold either, so her 'going out' must mean that the master's duty to support her ends. This gives a second law that matches the first: the master feeds the wife as well as the children.

phrases.english: In the same way you say:
"If he is a married man,
then his wife shall go out with him,"
Rabbi Shimon said:
If he was sold,
was his wife sold?
From here we learn that his master is obligated
to feed his wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same reasoning from step 18 to a parallel פסוק about the wife.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The master of a עבד עברי must support the servant's wife.

steps.title: Why the ברייתא needs to teach both wife and children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the case of the wife is needed, because from the children alone we might think a wife who can work should support herself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both are needed. If it had taught us only about his children, we would say that is because they cannot work and earn their food. But his wife can work and eat, so I might say: let her work and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a question it does not say out loud: why does the ברייתא need two similar teachings? It shows that the wife's case teaches something the children's case could not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Children cannot support themselves, so it makes sense that the master feeds them. A wife is able to work, so we might have thought she should earn her own food. The second teaching shows that the master must feed her for free too.

keyTerms.meaning: And it is necessary (to teach both cases)

steps.whatToRemember: The master supports both the servant's children and his wife. The wife's case is needed so we don't think that, because she can work, she has to earn her own food.

phrases.english: And it is necessary to teach both,
for if it had taught us only about his children,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא בְּנֵי מֶיעְבַּד וּמֵיכַל נִינְהוּ.
phrases.english: we would say that is because they are not able to work and earn their food.
But his wife,
who is able to eat and work,
I might say: let her work and eat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the ברייתא gives both the children case (step 18) and the wife case (step 19).
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each case teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the children alone, we might think a wife who can work must earn her own food.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wife's case is needed to teach that the master must feed her even though she is able to work.

steps.title: Why the children also had to be taught
steps.stepSummary: If we only knew about the wife, we might think the children do not need support, since children are used to going around asking for help. So both teachings are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the ברייתא had only taught us about the wife, we would say the master supports her because it is not her way to go around begging. But the children, who are used to going around, we would say he does not have to support. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its explanation from step 20 and shows the other direction: why the wife's case alone would not teach us about the children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 showed that the children's case alone would not cover the wife. Here the reverse is shown: a wife is too embarrassed to go asking for charity, so supporting her makes sense. Children are not embarrassed to ask, so we might think the master can leave them to go collecting. Each case has its own special reason, so רבי שמעון needs both.

keyTerms.meaning: It taught us, it let us hear
To go around, from door to door asking for help
Her way, what she normally does
I would say no (I might have thought the rule does not apply)
It is needed: both teachings are necessary

steps.whatToRemember: This is a classic צריכא: the wife and the children each have a different reason, so the master's duty to support each one must be taught separately.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only about his wife,
since it is not her way to go around,
phrases.notes: Going around means going door to door asking for charity.

phrases.english: but his children, whose way it is to go around,
I would say no, he need not support them,
therefore it is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the second half of the צריכא begun in step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each of two teachings is necessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the wife alone, we might think children, who are used to asking for charity, need not be supported.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both the wife and the children must be supported by the master, and each needs its own source.

steps.title: Opening a new teaching of the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא introduces a new ברייתא with the words תנו רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is about to quote a new ברייתא, and the words of that ברייתא come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תנו רבנן tells us a ברייתא from the time of the תנאים is being quoted. On its own it gives no ruling yet. It only prepares the next teaching.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the צריכא is finished, the גמרא moves on to a new ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduces a ברייתא; its content follows.
